title: Argumentation_framework
summary:
In artificial intelligence and related fields, an argumentation framework is a way to deal with contentious information and draw conclusions from it using formalized arguments. In an abstract argumentation framework, entry-level information is a set of abstract arguments that interact through attack relations.

The concept was pioneered by Phan Minh Dung in a seminal paper released in 1995. This work laid the foundation for understanding argument relations and bolstering the field of artificial intelligence. Given a set of arguments and an attack relation, one can build a directed graph and apply various semantics to determine which arguments are acceptable.

In logic-based argumentation frameworks, an argument is not an abstract entity but a pair, where the first part is a minimal consistent set of formulae sufficient to prove the formula in the second part. Given a particular attack relation, one can build a graph and reason similarly to abstract argumentation frameworks, with the difference being that the information inferred is a set of formulae representing consequences of accepted arguments.

Extensions represent consistent sets of arguments that can withstand attacks from outside their member arguments, contributing to the formation of valid conclusions. Several variants have been developed beyond the basic abstract framework, including bipolar argumentation frameworks (incorporating both support and conflict relations), weighted argumentation frameworks (assigning weights to arguments), and assumption-based argumentation frameworks. Applications include law, medicine, and multi-agent systems where formal logic and classical decision theory are unable to capture the richness of reasoning.
